summary: Catalogs experiences from developing infrastructure for a national, multi-organizational directory service and piloting it with off-the-shelf directory products.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is a report from a team that built a national directory service for Sweden and then ran it with real client and server software. It records what worked, such as answering searches within 10 seconds, and what did not, such as missing fields in standard directory schemas and clients that could not follow referrals. It is written as experience to pass on to others, not as a specification.

questions: what did the tisdag project learn
subtitle: What happened when a team built a national directory service for Sweden and ran it with real client and server software.

tldr.problem: A directory service that spans many organisations needs software that works with clients and servers that were never designed to talk to each other.
tldr.mechanism: The TISDAG project wrote two independent implementations of its specification and piloted them in the Swedish University Network with 10 directory servers behind the gateway, then recorded what worked and what did not.
tldr.outcome: The architecture worked as designed and answered queries within 10 seconds, but the team met limits in directory schemas, index compression, error reporting and commercial client software. The memo is Informational and offers those observations as guidance.

facts.label: Schemas used by the DAG system

today: RFC 2969 is an Informational memo recording the TISDAG team's experience from a pilot in October 2000, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. The memo describes the project as alive for a little over two years, with security support and schema flexibility named as the next steps. It is read with RFC 2967 and RFC 2968.

sections.title: The TISDAG Project and Its Goal
sections.content:
The TISDAG project, described in full in RFC 2967, set out to provide the infrastructure for a national whitepages directory service. To be effective, that infrastructure had to address the concrete realities of the client software end users already had, and the needs of the information providers, called Whitepages Directory Service Providers or WDSPs. Those realities include the existence of multiple protocols, both directory service access protocols and more general Internet application protocols such as HTTP and SMTP. The project was also sensitive to the fact that WDSPs have many good reasons for being reluctant to hand over copies of their subscribers' personal data.

The authors say these are their own observations, based on work done and general project discussions, and that other project participants probably have their own list of project experiences. The document is not claimed to be exhaustive.
sections.plainLanguage: The project aimed to give one country a single place to search for people and organisations, without every provider having to hand over its data. The memo explains what that meant in practice and what it cost.

sections.title: How the Gateway Is Built
sections.content:
The infrastructure gives end-user client software a place to run basic whitepages queries. Different connection points are provided for the protocols users are likely to want, which the memo lists as WWW, e-mail via SMTP, Whois++, LDAPv2 and LDAPv3. For each client, a transaction is carried out within the bounds of that protocol's syntax and semantics.

The system does not keep a replicated copy of all the whitepages information. It keeps an index over the data, which allows redirection, in the form of referrals, to services likely to contain a response that matches the client's query. The first and most important step is a query against the DAG Referral Index, a server holding index information obtained through the Common Indexing Protocol in the Tagged Index Object format. That index says which of the many participating WDSPs should be contacted to complete the query. Wherever possible the referrals are passed back to the querying client, so that it can contact the relevant WDSPs directly. That minimises the work done by the DAG system itself and gives WDSPs greater visibility. The protocols that support referrals natively are Whois++ and LDAPv3, and these may only be referred to servers of the same protocol.

Because many protocols do not support referrals, LDAPv2 among them, a second step called query chaining pursues those extra referrals inside the DAG system. The results from the different services are then packaged into a single response set for the client that made the query.

The components are separated by role. Client Access Points handle incoming queries from client software. A referral index maintains an index over the collected whitepages information and provides referrals based on actual data queries. Service Access Points mediate access to the WDSP servers to perform queries and retrieve results. At least one CAP and one SAP exist for every protocol supported for incoming queries and for WDSP servers respectively. The components were designed to be implementable as separate programs that talk to each other over an internal protocol, the DAG/IP, so that they can sit on different machines for load balancing and performance, and so that they have a common language for expressing queries and receiving results.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway keeps an index of what each provider can answer, not the answers themselves. A search is matched against that index, and the gateway then either points the client straight at the provider or fetches the answer itself and passes it back.

sections.title: What the Pilot Showed
sections.content:
Two independent implementations of the software were created, and a test deployment was set up within the Swedish University Network.

The system works pretty much as expected to provide transparent middleware for whitepages directory services. Client software and WDSP servers were minimally affected: from the point of view of behaviour and configuration, the DAG system looked like a server to clients and a client to servers.

The operational goal was to answer end-user queries in reasonable response times, although not to replace an address book. The prototype systems produced responses within 10 seconds, at least with the limited testbed of a configuration with 10 WDSPs providing directory service information. The memo also says the DAG system shows it is possible to build referral-level services at a national level, while noting that the deployment has yet to prove conclusively that it can operate as a transparent query-fulfillment proxy service in its current formulation.

Protocol mapping was demonstrated with N+M complexity instead of NxM mappings. Translations had to be defined for N allowable end-user query access protocols to and from the DAG/IP, and M supported WDSP server protocols, instead of requiring each of the N input components to map individually to the M output protocols. The prototype also showed some success in mapping between schema representations in the different protocol paradigms, in large part because the system's schemas were kept simple and focused on the minimal needs of the base service.
sections.plainLanguage: The design held up. Clients and providers needed few changes, and answers came back in about ten seconds. Translating between client protocols and provider protocols took one mapping per side rather than one for every pair.

sections.title: Where the Pilot Surprised the Team
sections.content:
Over the span of about a dozen months, from the first final document of the specification through implementation and first deployment, a few surprises surfaced. Some appeared when the theoretical specification was put into practice, and others when the resulting system was put into operation with commercial software clients and servers.

The first was that none of the standard LDAP person object classes included the organization attribute, o. The basic assumption seems to be that o will be part of the distinguished name for an entry, and therefore there is little cause to list it out separately. That makes it trickier to store information for people across multiple organizations, such as at an ISP's directory server, and to use the organization name in query refinement.

The second was the Tagged Index Object, used to carry indexes of provider information to the referral index. Its record tags are there to reduce the number of false positive referrals. Tag lists can get quite long depending on the ordering of the assignment of tags to the underlying data, so as the index grows the compression factor may not reach the efficiency of the simpler formats the design was modelled on. Sorting the underlying data before applying tags might produce a more compressed object, but it is not clear that this can be done efficiently over the whole set of records, attributes and tokens. Using the tags efficiently in the referral index also means reinflating the index object so that joins on tag lists can be done, which adds cost.

The third was handling status messages. When a query is chained to multiple WDSPs, it is not uncommon for at least one of them to return an error code or be unavailable. If one provider cannot be reached out of several referrals, should the client software be given the impression that the query completed successfully? Most client protocol error handling models are not sophisticated enough to make this level of distinction clear.

The fourth came from testing with standard commercial software. One client could handle only a very small subset of a protocol's defined status message lexicon, two system messages being the example given. Another automatically appended additional terms to a query the user had specified, for example adding or email= followed by what the user typed in.
sections.plainLanguage: Real software and real schemas did not match the specification. Some standard directory records had no field for the organisation, the index format grew less compactly than hoped, and some clients could not report errors properly or even changed the user's search.

sections.title: What Controls Speed and Index Size
sections.content:
The nature of the index object generated by the WDSPs has an important impact on performance, both in integrating the index object into the referral index and in the efficiency of handling queries. One proposal is to define more clearly how WDSPs should generate the CIP index object, which is currently left to their discretion, or to alert individual WDSPs when their index objects are considered substandard. When referrals are chained to WDSP servers, some servers perform more efficiently than others, which affects the overall response time of the DAG system, so it should also be possible to suggest to a WDSP that is consistently slow, longer than some selected response time, that it is substandard.

Several factors affect index size. If data is tokenized on names and addresses, that is, on data that is not unique like phone numbers, a rough estimate is that the number of tokens is 0.2 times the number of data records. The growth is linear from a few thousand up to at least 1.2 million records. It should then level off, since the sets of names and addresses are finite, but the tests had not shown a break point. If data is tokenized on something unique, such as phone numbers, the number of tokens is roughly the number of data records. Tokens are generated individually for each directory, so ten directories with 100,000 records generate the same amount of tokens as one directory with 1,000,000 records.

Several factors affect performance, measured in queries per second. A substring query is slower than an exact query, because the lookup in the internal DAG database is slower, more data is fetched because there are more hits, and the query is sent to the directory servers, which also return more data. A query with one or few attributes will most of the time result in many hits and a lot of data, while a query with many attributes results in a somewhat slower look-up in the internal database. A larger number of directories may result in many referrals and more data to process. Queries that are not chained are faster, since the result data does not have to be sent through the DAG system; chained queries to several directories can be processed in parallel in the SAPs, but all the data has to be processed in the CAP before it is sent to the client. The total response time for the DAG system is never faster than the slowest involved directory server. The number of tokens has little impact on the look-up time in the internal database.
sections.plainLanguage: How fast the gateway answers depends on the kind of search, how many attributes it carries, how many providers are involved, and how quickly the slowest provider replies. The index grows in proportion to the data and to the number of providers feeding it.

sections.title: Security and Next Steps
sections.content:
The project has so far focused on serving only publicly shareable information. The memo says any future work will have to provide additional facilities for authentication, authorization and encryption, and otherwise for handling sensitive data in an open environment. Section 4.1 makes the same point from the other side: security becomes necessary when the directory service is used in other application areas than the public white pages application, or even when it functions completely within an internal, closed network.

Two further directions are proposed. One is to let WDSPs use attributes and schemas the DAG system does not support today. The system currently uses two information schemas, DAGPERSON for information about specific people and DAGORGROLE for organizational roles, and the technical specification includes a definition of the schema as well as an understood mapping to and from some standard schemas used in the supported protocols. New WDSPs may not have all the attributes in these schemas, may use different schemas and query attributes, and may make local customisations, so it should be possible to create and use new customised or standardised schemas and perform schema mapping where it is necessary.

The memo's overall conclusion is that fewer people now hold out hope of a unified global directory service based on standardised protocols and schemas, while more projects provide infrastructure that permits unified access to what is otherwise a diverse and dislocated set of information servers. What cannot be dictated in protocols and schemas may yet be accommodated through service infrastructure, and the right approach seems to be to keep building frameworks for such services without making the framework architecture depend on specific technologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Only public data was served, so the pilot needed no security. Any wider use will need authentication, authorisation and encryption. The team also wanted providers to be able to use their own data formats instead of being forced into the system's two schemas.

cells: Standard LDAP person object classes carry the organization attribute
None of them did, so searching by organization returned nothing
The Tagged Index Object compresses as well as the simpler formats
Compression fell behind as the index grew, because tag lists got long
The client can tell that a query succeeded when only some providers answered
Most client error handling models cannot express that distinction
Client software handles the status messages its protocol defines
One client handled only two of them
